How It Could Go

The big numbers are the most likely real final score near the prediction, nudged toward scores football actually produces (24, 31, 17, 14 and 27 are common; 22 is six times rarer than 24). The averages underneath are the raw prediction, and close matchups land in the 20s. Real games miss the line by about 15 points either way, which is why one in five games has a team scoring 40+ and one in five has a team held under 14.

Why This Pick

Every number is points of final margin, added to whichever team is named. "Covered" means how a team did against the betting spread: +2 means it beat the spread by 2 points on average. "Trust" grows with sample size: games ÷ (games + 30), so 30 games is trusted halfway. Tap the i on any row to see its math.

Start hereWhat is the DAWG Index?

The DAWG Index grades every Power 4 game on whether a team showed up: beat the spread, finished drives, kept pulling away with a lead, cashed in after defensive stops and answered when the other team scored. Garbage time doesn't count, and road, night, packed-stadium and ranked-opponent games count more.

Download every graded game to check the work. It describes how teams played. It doesn't predict who wins or covers. For how a team is likely to play, see Tendencies. Tap any game to see how it graded.

Highlights

Big Games vs. Routine Games

Right = better than expected in routine games · Up = better in big games

Zero is an average team. Bigger dots have played more big games. Teams are spread out early in the season, and by December a dozen games pulls most of them toward the middle.

Coach Career follows the current head coach, not the school. It blends every season he's been a head coach since 2019, including previous jobs (Jon Sumrall's Troy and Tulane years count for Florida). Recent seasons count more (each year back is worth 80%), and short careers are pulled toward zero. Zero is a typical current Power 4 coach, since most of them were hired after beating expectations somewhere else. Dawg and Soft start at ±0.8 in this view instead of ±3.

Is DAWG Real?

If grit is a trait, a team's grade should carry over: good this year, good next year. If it's mostly luck, it should reset. Each number below runs from 0 (no carryover at all) to 1 (perfect). For reference, how good a team is carries over at about 0.5.

How the Grade Works

Big Games

Each game gets a stage score, the same for both teams except where noted: ranked opponent +15 (top 10 +25), ranked vs. ranked +10, rivalry +20, national TV (ABC, CBS, NBC, FOX, ESPN) +10, primetime on national TV +10 more, bowl, playoff or title game +30, neutral-site showcase +20, non-conference Power 4 matchup +10, packed stadium (90%+ of its biggest crowd, night crowds count 1.25×) +10, and an opponent that won 10+ games the season before +10. 25 or more is a big game, so it takes at least two of those. Contenders in big conferences play more of them, and that's intended.

Garbage time is out

Only competitive plays count. A play is garbage time when the lead before it is more than 38 in the 2nd quarter, 28 in the 3rd or 22 in the 4th. If the lead shrinks back under the line, plays count again, so a collapse still shows up.

vs spread

Did they beat the expectation set before kickoff? Home field is already priced in.

margin (no garbage time) + closing line

Finishing

Did the scoreboard match the yardage? Out-gaining a team and losing is a finishing gap.

margin − the margin those yards usually produce

Knife twist

Once up 9 or more, does the lead grow? Net points from that moment until garbage time, compared with what's normal for that matchup.

Cash-in

Points on the very next drive after the defense gets a stop or a takeaway, compared with what's normal for a team favored by that much. The national average is about 45% of those drives scoring.

Answers

When the opponent scores to make it a one-score game, how often does the next drive score?

The game grade

Each part is scored by how rare it is compared with every Power 4 game since 2019, so there's no ceiling: a 30-point cover counts for more than a 14-point one. Answers rests on a handful of drives, so it counts half as much as the other four. A game needs at least three of the five parts. The average is scaled so about two-thirds of games land between −5 and +5.

average of the five parts × setting

Setting

Bigger stages magnify the grade, good or bad: road +10%, night +5%, full road stadium (90%+, night crowds count 1.25×) +10%, ranked opponent +10% (top 10 +20%), postseason +10%. A good grade against a Group of 5 team shrinks 15%, against an FCS team 40%; a bad grade against them is never softened.

Season DAWG and big-stage drop

A season's DAWG is the average of its game grades, with 0 as an average Power 4 team. +3 or better is Dawg, −3 or worse is Soft. Big-game and routine averages leave out the setting boost, so a team doesn't look like it rose just because the stage was bigger. With only a game or two, those averages are nudged toward the team's overall number so one game can't put a team at the edge of the chart.

big-stage drop = big-game grade − routine grade

Luck

Wins minus the wins a team's play earned. Each game's win chance comes from the play-by-play with garbage time removed: how often plays succeeded, explosive plays, penalties, turnovers forced and given away, and field-goal tries judged by distance. The parts that are mostly chance (who falls on a fumble, interception swings, missed kicks, return touchdowns) are left out, so they show up as luck. +2 means two more wins than the play earned. Lucky teams tend to come back to earth.

Data: ESPN box scores, drive logs and closing lines (ESPN BET and DraftKings) for every game involving a current Power 4 team or Notre Dame since 2019, including bowls and playoffs. Coaches from Wikipedia's list of current FBS coaches. Attendance is missing for some games; those use a 75% default.

Check the work: download every graded game (CSV, one row per team per game, with each part of the grade). It's updated every Sunday with the site.
